speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank you very much and I wish to express my appreciation to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for the good wishes extended to me on this occasion. I do feel that evidence of friendship extended in this way is a happy expression of the real and deep friendships which do exist in this house and which are in no way affected by the sometimes strenuous differences of opinion which are expressed in regard to public affairs. That neither diminishes our convictions in relation to the subjects we are discussing nor does it diminish the effectiveness of our contribution. On the contrary, I think it is a happy thing that all of us with different political opinions may meet here and respect those differences and yet build warm friendships which I hope will last for all of us through the rest of our lives.

FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I beg
leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis):
The adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the advisability of this house expressing its opinion on the method to be employed in the financing of the western portion of an across-Canada gas pipe line.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar has just moved the adjournment of the house under standing order 26. The matter that he wishes to bring to the attention of the house is:
The method to be employed in the financing of the western portion of an across-Canada gas pipe line.
A matter to be dealt with on a motion of this kind has to be a definite matter. I wonder how definite it is to discuss the method of financing of the western portion of an across-Canada gas pipe line. Furthermore, as hon. members know, there is on the order paper a resolution which has already been taken up in committee of the whole and it certainly deals with the financing of a portion of a pipe line, called the trans-Canada pipe line, in the northern section of the province of Ontario. Of course, if there is to be further financing for another portion of the line another resolution will have to be introduced.

At this moment I am asking myself if the purpose of this motion today is not to ask the house to give its opinion on a matter which is usually introduced in the house after notice. A question of financing is one that must be introduced by a resolution recommended by the governor general.
I have no doubt that before the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar decided to make this move today he looked at the authorities and felt assured that the move was in order. In the circumstances he would certainly be of great assistance to me if he would tell me whether it is his contention, after having looked at the authorities, that whatever I have said so far is, as far as he is concerned, of no value whatever.

subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I am very glad to do that. First of all, I will take your point that this matter is already on the order paper. I would draw your attention to the fact that it is not covered by the resolution on the order paper nor by any discussion we have had in the house up to the present time. As for the urgency of the situation, I think that even a casual reader of the press will realize that this matter has some urgency, and because of the apparent internal situation within the government itself it seems to me that the time has arrived when the members of the house should give some consideration to the matter. The urgency is, I may say, also due to the fact that the agreement regarding the trans-Canada pipe line as such has, as far as the province of Ontario is concerned, already lapsed. It is true that there has been an extension by the federal authority but there has been no extension by the government of the province of Ontario.
Since this matter has been under advisement for five years and apparently no conclusion has been reached and because of the state of public opinion regarding it in the country and as shown by the press, I think the time has arrived when, if the government cannot come to a conclusion, this house should take a hand in this very important and serious matter from the point of view of the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: On the point of order, it seems to me that we are doing by indirection what cannot be done by direction. The leader of the C.C.F. party is seeking to have an expression of opinion in favour of an expenditure of money for a particular purpose which can only be recommended by the government to the house.

subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That is not in the motion.

subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Who said that?
[Mr. Harris.)

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Then I am not just sure what else could be in the motion except that. If my hon. friend makes the point that he does not propose to seek to have the house declare itself in favour of a public ownership system, then I am not aware of what the point of the motion is. In the resolution before the house we are proposing a certain limited form of financing for a part of the line. It has already been indicated by the group for which my hon. friend speaks that they intend to oppose that plan on the ground that they think it ought to be publicly financed throughout. If that is a defence and objection to the resolution on the order paper, then I do not think the rules permit a second debate by having a motion to adjourn the house to discuss that very point.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I point out that the urgency which in our opinion now faces the house and the country relates not to the matter covered by the government motion on the order paper, namely the line through northern Ontario, but rather to getting something done without further delay in western Canada. This motion merely suggests that the house should without further delay discuss the method to be employed in financing a line in western Canada, the purpose being so that the government might have the benefit of the discussion here in the house.

subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Hon. members laugh; but the very members who are laughing realize that the government needs the benefit of some advice. Your Honour realizes that the urgency that confronts us today is that unless some action is taken before long the western leg of the across-Canada pipe line cannot be built this year. Because of that urgency we feel that the house should have a chance today to express its opinion in debate on the matter. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) raises the question as to the authority of the house on a private member's motion in the matter of an expenditure of money. It is perfectly correct that a private member could not move a motion involving the expenditure of money. That is the reason we ask not for a decision on a motion but for a chance to discuss this matter so that hon. members may lay before parliament their views on the rumours as to what the government has in mind or their views as to what they feel should be done to get this project under way without further delay.

subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) said that this motion apparently intended to do by indirection that which could not be
Pipe Lines-Financing done by direction, if I understood him correctly. As a matter of fact, I think it is the other way around. This motion intends to give the government the benefit of the direction of the House of Commons in order to avoid the results of the indirection that has characterized the government for so long. Hence it is indeed a matter of urgent importance, for we find ourselves today in a position in which every hour, on the hour, the press of this country-and it has been singularly correct in its assumptions and conclusions-is informing parliament as to what has taken place with regard to this matter. I feel that this is a matter of urgent importance in order to clarify the atmosphere and to ascertain the degree to which there has indeed been withheld from parliament information that parliament had a right to receive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Just in order to clear up the final point, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. It seems to me that when the present resolution on the order paper with respect to Trans-Canada is called for discussion, every avenue of discussion with respect to the building, the financing or the like is open to opposition members. It may be true-although I do not think in this house we accept these statements at face value-that it is the case that the western section will not be built this summer unless certain action is taken immediately. But in any event that is not a reason for urgency. The urgency is on the matter of debate and the urgency of debate is only in case there cannot be another occasion for a debate. On the Trans-Canada resolution all these things can be said.

subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: You are embarrassed.

subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, following on the remarks of the Minister of Finance, I would refer you to the actual wording of the resolution on the order paper. You will find that it is a resolution apparently for the introduction of a measure to provide for the constitution of the corporation to be known as the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation. Mr. Speaker, I would be greatly surprised if, when the matter is being debated, the Minister of Finance were not on his feet quickly if some hon. member attempts to debate something beyond the purview of that resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: It has already been done and I did not object.

subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I think this motion is a very timely one because it is certainly a matter of urgent importance that work be started on the western end of this pipe line at the very earliest date possible.

Pipe Lines-Financing

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
May I thank hon. members for the consideration that they have given to this matter. I come back to the point I raised earlier about the word "definite". I am reading the motion now, not because I accept it, but I am reading it to myself in order to analyse the terms-"... adjournment of the house be moved under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent public importance." According to standing order 26 the word "definite" means that the matter must be one that is specific and well defined.
In this case we have as the definite matter a reference to a method of financing. Now, how many methods of financing are there, and upon which one is the house going to express an opinion? In debate, it is true, there will be many methods of financing mentioned but I think that the method of financing should have been defined in the motion. Then, the motion refers to an across-Canada pipe line; it presupposes there will be an across-Canada pipe line.
Then, there is the reference to a matter of urgent public importance and I stress the word "urgent". Hon. members have referred to the urgency of having a pipe line built across western Canada. Hon. members know that here the word "urgent" does not apply to the project itself but it applies to the debate. Is there urgency of debate? The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said this matter has been under consideration for five years, and between now and the end of the session there will be other opportunities for debate.
I would ask hon. members to look at citation 176 of Beauchesne's third edition, page 77, which reads:
The "definite matter of urgent public importance", for the discussion of which the adjournment of the house may be moved under standing order 31,-
That is now standing order 26.
-must be so pressing that public interest will suffer if it is not given immediate attention.
I ask hon. members, is the method of financing a matter that is so pressing that the public interest will suffer if it is not given immediate attention today?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. member and I may feel that way, that whatever is on the order paper today appointed for discussion should be put aside in order to discuss this matter. The urgency of this motion applies to the debate, and I am inclined to think there will be opportunities shortly for the discussion of this matter. Of course, it is of public importance and it is urgent in the sense that

all Canadians wish to keep things moving. We are a progressive, expanding country, and we all want to do things as soon as possible. But is there urgency of debate in connection with this motion? I am inclined to think there is not.

subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a question-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I have heard comments from several hon. members, and when I rose I took it that all those who had something to offer had expressed their views. I believe hon. members will have to bear with me when I say that I think if they do not want to be too harsh on their Speaker they will have to consider whether or not, every time he makes a ruling, they have to argue every point he puts forward. I am making a ruling now and it is not debatable nor appealable. Let us stop having that traditional rule that Speaker's rulings are not debatable be an illusion.
The other point I wish to make is that the matter must be one of recent occurrence. This is a matter that has been dealt with everywhere, in the press and in this house for many, many months now. I come to the conclusion that in my humble view this is not a matter of urgent public importance in the sense which is traditionally the one known to be the sense in standing order 26 and therefore I do not accept the motion.

subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Did you say that your ruling would be appealed, Mr. Speaker? That is not my understanding. If it is your opinion it can be appealed-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: FINANCING-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: No. We settled that on Friday. I want to say that precisely because of the strength the hon. member gave me I feel fortified and I can assure him that as far as I am concerned any decision that I make under standing order 26 will not be appealable as long as I am Speaker. That is quite definite.

This reminds me of a statement I made not very long ago on the matter of asking questions based on reports appearing in the press. Beauchesne says that if a member bases a question on a report that has appeared in the press he must make himself responsible for its accuracy. I said at that time that as there was no penalty for irresponsibility I did not think the rule meant very much and that the citation was meaningless. It so happens that I was told that it was not meaningless. I received private and confidential advice from a very high authority to the effect that when

Inquiries of the Ministry a member uses a press report he must make himself absolutely responsible for its accuracy and if it turns out that the report on which he bases himself in putting his question to the house is not accurate he is abusing the rules of the house. Now that I have had that advice, which is contrary to what I had thought was the correct interpretation of the citation, I should like hon. members to think that one over because it seems to me that the practice is wrong.
Any newspaperman who is not a member of the house may write anything in the newspapers that he feels like writing. If hon. members are to take for granted that because a certain statement has appeared in the press it is right and they do not make themselves responsible for whatever questions they base on such articles and ask such questions in the house, we are going to lose a tremendous amount of time. subsubtopic: SEIZURE OF CANADIAN VESSELS ON LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries. Can the minister say whether a Canadian fishing vessel on lake Erie was fired upon and hit three times by a United States patrol? Also can the minister say whether the Ontario fishermen's association lodged a protest with the federal government over what the manager has termed an unprovoked and unnecessary attack on a Canadian craft?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subsubtopic: SEIZURE OF CANADIAN VESSELS ON LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member refers to Friday's Hansard he will find that I answered the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) with regard to that matter.

subsubtopic: SEIZURE OF CANADIAN VESSELS ON LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is it still the minister's opinion that the shot that was fired went over the bow, as he suggested last Friday, and did not in fact hit any vessel?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subsubtopic: SEIZURE OF CANADIAN VESSELS ON LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for the information of the hon. member from the prairies may I say that shots are not fired over the bow; they are fired across the bow. As I reminded the house on Friday, this is the accepted way of halting a ship in order to put it under arrest. Our own ships on both coasts do it with regard to our Canadian nationals and also with regard to American nationals who occasionally drift across our boundaries. Just as the police, in order to stop motor vehicles, sound their sirens, in the case of vessels a shot is fired across the bow.

subsubtopic: SEIZURE OF CANADIAN VESSELS ON LAKE ERIE

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC AND BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Before this motion is carried, Mr. Speaker, I just wish to refer to a statement which was made on Thursday last during the debates. At that time I took exception to the remarks made by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who inferred that probably the action of the provincial government in reducing the number of their judges was not motivated entirely out of consideration for the relative demands of justice nor for the necessity that justice be obtained with all possible speed. I made objection at that time. Since that time I have been in contact with the attorney general of the province. He issued a statement to the effect that the hon. member for Prince Albert was wrong on a number of points. First, it was not within two years that the legislation was passed but that it was passed in 1951-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC AND BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: That is right. It was in 1951.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC AND BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
-and not in 1953 which would be two years ago. The second point on which he was wrong was in the inference that the Saskatchewan government, in reducing the number of judges of Queen's Bench was in some way taking action to prevent the appointment of a judge who was a member of this house. The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) was at that time the leader of the Liberal opposition in the province of Saskatchewan. I do not think he had any intention of trying to become a member of the bench or to be appointed to the bench. At that time he was doing his best to become premier of the province of Saskatchewan. He fought very hard and I think he probably put up a good fight. But we cannot take the charge that the government of Saskatchewan was moving in any way to hurt the administration of justice in that province. As a matter of fact, while the hon. member for Prince Albert states that he might be desiring to become a member of the bench or to be appointed thereto, I think it should be pointed out that at that time when the hon. member for Rosthern was sitting in the house in the province of Saskatchewan and when this legislation was brought down, he supported it as every member of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan at that time supported it. It should also be pointed out that the attorney general in


the province of Saskatchewan and the government of that province were acting entirely in the best interests of the province. As the attorney general stated in his press release:
We felt in the public interest and in fairness to the taxpayers, as each judge costs nearly $20,000 annually, that the number of judges should be kept in line with the judicial work to be done. Apparently Mr. Tucker agreed because as house leader of the Liberal opposition he voted for the legislation as did all Liberals in the house.
I think the hon. member for Prince Albert would perhaps like to get to his feet and state that it was not his intention to cast any reflections on the province of Saskatchewan and their motives in having the number of judges reduced in that province at that time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC AND BRITISH COLUMBIA

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SALARIES FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGES IN QUEBEC AND BRITISH COLUMBIA

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
I do not want to pursue this matter any further as far as going into the detail is concerned. I do, however, want to ask the minister whether or not, on the basis of the experience of some years in the operation of the transport controller's office, it is the intention of his department to amplify, expand or extend the purview of any of the regulations that were passed in order to make this legislation effectual. I do so because of the circumstances brought to the minister's attention when this matter was up for debate, that there had not been that enforcement of the regulations which their amplitude would permit. I am wondering, in view of the experience that has taken place in connection with the allotments that have brought a measure of serious
Department of Transport Act injustice to various marketing points in Saskatchewan and the other prairie provinces, whether there is any intention to alter, amend or otherwise change any of the provisions of the regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is no intention to make any change in the regulations at this time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
Since this matter was
before us last week, the Minister of Trade and Commerce made an important announcement in connection with the policy on deliveries. It so happens that my constituency is in a favourable freight rate region with reference to the port of Churchill. In the past it has been the policy to hold a considerable volume of grain in the area of my constituency to have it accessible to Churchill when the ships arrive. It was possible, in the past, to make some adjustment after the new crop was begun so that the people in that area could send some wheat to Churchill. According to the new policy-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
I should like to raise a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I know that during the resolution stage of this bill we had a very full discussion of a number of matters which were more or less related to the question of transport control. Then, on second reading of the bill we went through exactly the same process. It seemed to me that was quite in order because at that particular time the house was considering the principle which was at issue in this bill, should transport control be extended for two years.
The house has passed second reading unanimously, which I take it meant there was a unanimous decision that transport control should be continued for two years. It seems to me, therefore, that although the situation at Churchill may be interesting and although it may have been relevant at an earlier stage, in view of the decision of the house that control should be extended for two years my contention is that we are now considering how it should be extended for two years and whether the bill does or does not do that. The house has already decided that control should be continued for two years, so it is my contention that a discussion of the situation in Churchill is not relevant to the bill before the committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
May I ask whether it is possible to make a distinction between what was in order on second reading and what is in order in committee of the whole on the bill, in view of the fact the bill means the same thing at the two points, namely whether it is in order to continue the powers of the

Department of Transport Act transport controller. Surely, if it were in order to discuss the powers of the controller on second reading of the bill, the same thing should be in order now.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
I think the committee as a whole appreciates the point the minister was endeavouring to make that there is a difference-I think there is a difference-between the general discussion of principle which is always allowed on second reading and the very specific discussion we are supposed to have under standing order 59 (2) which says that speeches in committee of the whole must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
At the same time I have to realize that while the only change being made in this section is the change from the words 1956 to 1958, it does have the effect of extending the life of section 6A of the Department of Transport Act. I cannot really rule that a discussion of the activities of an official appointed under that section would be out of [DOT]order. At the same time I think I would be justified, and perhaps I should endeavour to hold the discussion more practically to its effect on transport than to its secondary effect [DOT]on the marketing and storage of wheat. I feel confident that members of the house, having thoroughly discussed the bill, are anxious that discussion now should be orderly and practical. I think perhaps from there we can go on without too much difficulty.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
I am very glad, Mr. Chairman, that you did not rule me out of order. I submit the argument I am about to make is valid and it is related to a new situation which was not before us either in the resolution stage or the debate on second reading of the bill.
I was pointing out that 20 per cent of the points in Saskatchewan were on a one-bushel quota, and in Manitoba one quarter of 1 per cent were on a one-bushel quota; in Alberta, 3 per cent were on a one-bushel quota. The Minister of Trade and Commerce announced that the year 1956-57 is to be unlike any previous year when the transport controller was permitted to try his best to see that the allocation was fair all across the prairie provinces. It so happens my constituency is an area where we have a very low quota, partly because the grain is being held there to have it available for Churchill when shipping opens out of that northern port.
In previous years, as a result of having the period extended, it was possible in August and even September to have grain accepted in that area and handled on the previous year's quota. A real hardship is being experienced in that area where they have this


very low quota now, and if something is not done between now and the end of the present crop year to give them a chance to get grain out that hardship will be even worse. I submit this regulation is also going to work an injustice at Churchill. It is going to make it very difficult to hold sufficient grain in that area to supply the ships with their cargoes, since the shipping season opens later in Hudson bay than it does in Vancouver and in the eastern ports. I submit that the minister must give directions to the transport controller to take into consideration the new factors which were announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce last week, which have been partly ignored in the past, and make it possible for the people in all sections of the prairie provinces to be able to look forward to getting their fair quota out some time before the end of the crop year.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
I also think that the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day shows that it is necessary that an altogether new type of policy regarding the allocation of box cars be introduced. The minister said that there were 14 stations on the 1-bushel quota, 478 on a 2-bushel quota, 572 on a 3-bushel quota, 602 on a 4-bushel quota and 400 on a 5-bushel quota. It is very hard to understand how it is that some of those points were allowed to have a 4 and 5-bushel quota while other points had only a 1-bushel quota.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce told the house that it may not be possible to attain a uniform quota before the end of the crop year' 1955-56. He said that all quotas in effect on July 31, 1956, would expire on that date. Therefore, I think the minister will agree it is very essential from now on that no more cars should be allocated to those points that have a 4 and 5-bushel quota until such time as the points with a quota of one or two bushels have been brought up to the 4 and 5-bushel level. The whole trouble arises from the fact that we have this peculiar situation. The wheat board has the responsibility for allocating orders but it has no authority. The transport controller has the authority to allocate cars but it has no responsibility to give the orders which will move the cars to those points. It seems to me we must have a man somewhere with not only the responsibility but also the authority to carry out that responsibility. So long as we have two different people, one with the responsibility and the other with the authority, we are bound to have just the same kind of confusion and chaos that we have at the present time. Therefore, I am hoping the minister will be able to instruct the transport controller that in future cars will have to

be allocated in such a way that those points that are still on the 1 and 2-bushel quota shall receive cars until such time as they are brought up on a level with the points that have a 4 and 5-bushel quota.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext: Has the minister discovered many instances where the transport controller has found that his directives to railway companies have not been fulfilled? The condition which has resulted in several points in the province with which I am particularly familiar is that on main line points, particularly on the C.N.R., there appears to be a sufficient number of box cars available, but on branch line points-and this is true in my own area-of the C.P.R. the farmers find it very difficult to get cars and when they do get the cars they find it difficult to get a proper allocation. If there appear to be cars required at certain points it has been reported to me that a certain elevator had shipping orders and another elevator belonging to a line company had no shipping orders. The line company got the cars without the shipping orders and the wheat pool elevator with shipping orders could not get cars. The cars were allocated on the basis of one to one. I do not think that condition should occur. I was wondering whether or not it was the result of the railways failing to carry out a directive of the transport controller? What action could the transport controller take if he found that his directives to a railway company were not being carried out? Suppose he asked them to direct cars to certain shipping points on a branch line because of the congestion of wheat there, because there was a backlog of shipping orders or shipments out from that point, what would happen?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
All I can say is that so far as I am aware only one directive has been issued by the transport controller. Information was given, I think last year, in reply to a question asked in the house, but I know of only one which was issued, and I do not know whether that was issued under section 6A of the Department of Transport Act or whether it was issued under the regulations that existed previously. However, I do not think there is any doubt that the regulations provide adequate penalties for the failure to carry out directives. I am quite sure the hon. member will understand that legally one should make a distinction between an order which is given by the transport controller over the telephone, and which the railway promises to carry out and does carry out, and a formal order. I do not think anybody looks on that as qualifying as being a directive. When it is reduced to writing and put
Department of Transport Act in a formal way to the railway, then it becomes a directive. As I say, only one of those has been issued. I am sure all hon. gentlemen will realize that the facility with which a telephone call can be converted into a formal directive makes a telephone call very effective.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
Can the
minister give us some assurance that he will instruct the present transport controller to take his responsibilities more seriously than he has in the past to see that box cars are moved into those points where wheat board orders are now available? It does seem to me that if this situation is allowed to continue the Canadian wheat board will be taking the blame for the failure to move the grain from the west when, as far as I can see it, it is not the body that is responsible for seeing that box cars are spotted after orders have been given. I do know this. There are certain powers in the west and throughout Canada generally who would like to see the Canadian wheat board discredited. I have the feeling that unless this government does something to clarify this matter and to say, for example, to the transport controller, "Now, you see that box cars are moved into those points that have shipping orders from the wheat board and at the time they are given", the wheat board will get the blame. If that is done the Canadian wheat board will not be subject to the rough time they are experiencing through no fault of their own.
Is the minister prepared to give this committee some assurance that he will instruct the present transport controller to exercise the power which this act gives him to a greater degree than he has in the past? As the minister pointed out, he did not have the responsibility to do it. The minister should tell us right now that he is going to instruct the transport controller to take it as his responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall merely answer by saying that in order to carry out a proper and efficient job in moving wheat to export points we must have the closest degree of collaboration between the Canadian wheat board and the transport controller himself. I would be unwilling to give the assurance in the terms which the hon. member has just suggested. I think that so long as marketing is the responsibility of the Canadian wheat board wheat can be moved most efficiently when the transport controller cooperates closely with the Canadian wheat board and sees jointly with the board and with the railway companies that the cars

Department of Transport Act are put in the right place at the right time. I do not think I can go farther than that, Mr. Chairman.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
I know of cases where the wheat board has given shipping orders to certain points. I have in mind one particular place where there were 42 orders for shipment. I took this matter up with the transport controller away back in February and he told me that was not part of his duty but that he would watch this particular subdivision. Over the weekend I received a statement of the various quotas established in my particular part of the province and I find that there are four points still on a two-bushel quota. Those four points lie along the branch line which the transport controller assured me he would look after.
It is not a case of the grain not being there, it is not a case of wheat board orders not being there, it is simply that the C.P.R. has failed to move in the box cars. It is situations like that that I would like to have straightened out. The minister should instruct the transport controller to keep a close watch on what is going on throughout western Canada.
Before closing, I should like to substantiate the remarks made by the hon. member for Acadia. The announcement that was made last Thursday makes the movement of wheat from western points of urgent importance. I hope that something will be done before July to see that all points in the west are able to market their fair quotas and certainly that we do not again get into a mess such as the one we saw last winter.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, arising out of the minister's statement and now that this subject is being discussed at some length-
I thought it was going to be restricted-may I ask the minister, having regard to the statement he made a litttle while ago that the achievement of the best possible allocation of cars in a just and perfect way would come about through close co-operation between the transport controller and the wheat board, if there has not been that co-operation and if that is the explanation for the diversity of distribution of cars and the fact that adjoining towns find themselves in a position where there is no degree of justice and where fair distribution has not been attained. I do not belong to those who believe in making attacks upon individuals who cannot defend themselves. I do not believe in taking advantage of my position in the House of Commons to refer to individuals outside the house who cannot answer in their own defence. I ask the minister


whether there has been that co-operation which he advised us was of the essence of a good and proper distribution, or whether in his opinion much could be done to improve that spirit of co-operation to which he referred so warmly?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext: I do not think it could be implied from anything I said that there is not the fullest co-operation between the transport controller and the Canadian wheat board. In fact I feel perfectly convinced that if there had not been that kind of collaboration the transport controller and the railroads would not have been able to have done as successfully as they have in these last winter months the job of transport that has been accomplished. I was not referring particularly to relations in the past between Mr. Milner and the wheat board; I merely was endeavouring to reply to the hon. gentleman opposite by indicating that I did not believe that a literal adherence by the transport controller to the regulations would procure the best results. I believe the best results will be procured, as I said a moment ago, when there is a high degree of collaboration between the transport controller and the wheat board which could be translated into procuring from the railroads the necessary box cars to carry our wheat to points for export.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext: A reading between the lines of what the minister has said may offer an explanation for the incongruous position that has arisen in the distribution of box cars, beginning with the first of last August and continuing until January 18 or 20, at which time there was some improvement. I am not going to pursue this matter further except to say that the minister might give a little fatherly advice as to the needs of the western farmer with the laudable desire in mind of seeing that a similar iniquitous situation shall not again arise this coming fall when the farmers in certain areas might find themselves to all intents and purposes discriminated against or certainly denied their fair and equitable share of the distribution of box cars.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext: I think if somebody would give fatherly advice to the opposition and tell them not to ask questions which have been asked before it would be most timely at the present time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
It is rather hard to find who is responsible as among these three bodies. Even in the railway committee we had the greatest difficulty in finding out who was responsible. In connection with directives, we were informed that there had been no directives issued to the railway companies

by the controller. Then Mr. Gordon said that he would admit no responsibility. He said that they had nothing to do with this, that they just did what they were told. I have a picture of Mr. Gordon doing what he is told, but that is by the by.
Then when we inquired into the situation as between the railroads and the transport *controller we were given a description of a sort of loose liaison such as that which the minister has described. Somebody would pick up a telephone and talk to somebody at the other end and they apparently would come to some sort of amicable agreement.
As the hon. member behind me has said, there should be some definite responsibility so that we would know where public criticism should be directed. When I say that, I do not mean virulent attacks such as those referred to by the hon. member for Prince Albert. There should be some final responsibility.
I have heard the situation described as a dodging of responsibility or, in the vernacular, a passing of the buck. There should be some definite way of fixing responsibility in connection with this undeniably dangerous and uneconomic situation which existed in certain places last winter and which still exists in many points on the prairies.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was glad to hear the minister state that there was going to be a degree of collaboration between the transport controller and the Canadian wheat board, but I would have preferred to have had him use the word "cooperation". I have two specific questions which I should like to ask. Seeing that there is this collaboration between the wheat board and the transport controller, to whom would individuals, say members of wheat pool committees or interested farmers, address their grievances? For example, if there is a shortage of shipping orders at a marketing point, do they draw it to the attention of the Canadian wheat board? Further, if there are adequate shipping orders at a marketing point but insufficient box cars, is that then drawn to the attention of the transport controller?
I think we must define this collaboration, and I would ask the minister to answer those two questions and indicate to me that, if there is a shortage of shipping orders, then that is the responsibility of the Canadian wheat board, but, if there is a shortage of box cars, then that is the responsibility of the transport controller.
Last Wednesday I brought a case to the attention of the minister and pointed out that a marketing point was only on a three-bushel quota. I followed his advice and took it up
Department of Transport Act with the Canadian wheat board, who informed me there were 26 outstanding shipping orders. I presume that that becomes the aspect of the collaboration that concerns the transport controller. I hope I am right in my assumption that individuals in the country will make their appeals to the transport controller or to the wheat board, depending on whether there is a shortage of box cars or a shortage of shipping orders.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext: I think the hon. member has answered his own questions.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF AUTHORITY TO MAKE REGULATIONS AND APPOINT CONTROLLERS
speechtext:
Someone says that the hon. member for Kindersley might be able to get a better answer that way. It seems to be generally agreed that there has been some real difficulty in moving the grain in recent months, and it is being said that there was an improvement about last January. If we could look forward to continued improvement, if we could look forward to these anomalies of which we have been speaking being removed, if we could look forward to equitable quotas being forthcoming, then there would not be any need for us to take part in this discussion. But it seems to me that right at this moment there is very gross discrimination in the allocation of box cars and that the efforts of the wheat board and the efforts, perhaps to a considerable extent, of the transport controller himself are being thwarted and being set aside by the failure of the railway companies to co-operate and to supply the box cars and to allocate them in a fair and equitable manner.
I am afraid that the railway companies are doing a very grave disservice at this time in their handling of box-car allocation and distribution to the Canadian wheat board itself, because it is a fact that there is not a fair allocation of box cars, either among shipping points or among the producers at shipping points. We had only last Thursday the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to the distribution of wheat delivery quotas at this time. Those figures have been put on the record. Fourteen points were on a one-bushel quota; 478 points on a two-bushel quota; 572 points on a three-bushel quota; 602 points on a four-bushel quota; 400 points on a five-bushel quota. That is a very unfair distribution of quotas at this moment. I trust that steps will be taken to bring these quotas together within a few months. But what bothers me is the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce last Thursday, in which he took a very large part of the time used in delivering a rather comprehensive statement to the house on the grain situation to inform us that there would not be, at the end of July, any steps taken to equalize

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the parliamentary assistant has said, this bill has been before the banking and commerce committee and there is not a great deal that one can or should say about it. I should like to make one or two general observations to remind us that in our glorious boom that gives us such immense satisfaction there are some people who are not sharing, notably the farming industry. I do not propose to weary the committee with a lot of figures. We have been over that ground a good deal. This bill is an attempt to deal in a rather inadequate way, I suggest, with the problem.
I often wonder whether we take it seriously enough. My own feeling is that no prosperity that does not include the farmers can be durable or satisfactory although of course the day is past when nobody can be a success unless he has been born in the country and walked four miles every day to school. We have got to the stage now when such a large percentage of the population is non-agricultural that the farm dwellers no longer provide the percentage of leaders in the community that they used to. Nevertheless I should like to correct any feeling we may have that the farm industry is not important by saying that I myself think it is of great importance and also-and much more significantly-by quoting to you two or three things which have been said by well-known people about the farming industry. The great French writer Rousseau says "The first and most respectable of all the arts"-you will notice, Mr. Chairman, that he calls it an art-"is agriculture". The well-known American Daniel Webster says this:
Let us never forget that the cultivation of the earth is the most important labour of man.
But the quotation I should like to impress upon hon. members is one which I am sure will interest them, because it refers to the calling of those of us who are at present seated in this chamber. It comes from the sharp tongue of Swift and is taken from *"Gulliver's Travels":
And he gave it for his opinion, that whoever could make two ears of corn, or two blades of .grass, to grow upon a spot of ground where only-one grew before, would deserve better of mankind,


and do more essential service to his country, than the whole race of politicians put together.
I have quoted that excerpt just so it may reduce us to a proper state of humility, Mr. Chairman, and also as a preface to dealing with the efforts of the politicians to help with regard to the farm problem. I think we can say-and I repeat it-that agriculture is lagging behind in prosperity. We have discussed in this chamber the problems with regard to wheat, cheese and butter, and I need not dwell upon them. So far as this board is concerned, my criticism is not that the work has not been well done. I think the board has done the work well. They have done it, at any rate, carefully and prudently. If a criticism could be made, perhaps it is that they have been too prudent.
My criticism is that I think the basic purpose of the board has rather been lost sight of. My feeling is that this board should regard itself as a public service board whereas, so far as I can make out, it seems to have regarded itself-and to have been allowed to do so-primarily as a profit-making institution. When I say "primarily" what I mean is that I think those running the board have had it much in their minds that they were obliged to show a substantial margin on the right side.
That perhaps is partly because of the circumstances of its organization. At that time they talked about profit and dividends whereas, when the housing act was before this house, I suggest that what was being considered was service to those who needed service with, of course, a proper regard for the safeguarding of public investment. There, much more than with regard to the operation of this farm loan board, I think was the feeling that the legislation was primarily a matter of public service.
Again I am not going to give a large number of figures. However, if we turn to the statement of the board we find that in the year 1955 the board had net earnings of $162,000 and that they paid income tax of $73,000. I think there is a certain irony in that fact. When we come to crown corporations that are in the business of making money and selling goods, that are in the business of competing in the open market with others such as, let us say, the Polymer Corporation, it seems to me that there, when you are in ordinary business-I was going to say "competitive business" but I suppose Polymer is largely a monopoly; but at any rate it is competing with other products if with nothing else-I suggest that considerations arise which do not and should not arise in the case of what I suggest should be an

organization serving the public. I am not going to pursue that point.
Let me say again that I think the chairman of the farm loan board has been carrying on the operations of the board as he was intended to carry them on, namely to make a profit. He has done that, and I have no doubt he felt that he was entitled to feel that that was his job. Having said that I do not propose to dwell at length on the matter. There were certain main points of discussion which arose and which will no doubt be discussed further this afternoon.
The three points of change in the bill were mainly the valuation, which under the bill is increased to 65 per cent; that is to say, loans may be made up to 65 per cent of value. Amendments suggesting that the percentage should be higher than that were moved in the committee and were defeated. The second matter was the total amount of loans. There again there was a question in the committee and an amendment raising the amount was moved and defeated. In the third place there was the question of the duration of the loan. As to that matter, the government accepted an amendment raising it from 25 years to 30 years. I think perhaps it would be more sensible to discuss the other two points-that is to say the raising of the valuation figure and the ceiling on the loan-when we come to the relevant clauses. I shall therefore defer my comments until then.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is essential to the agricultural industry that we have a type of long-term mortgage credit at reasonable rates of interest. The whole question of financing the purchase and sale of farms is different from the financing generally of other businesses in the nation. It is different, first of all, because you have a rather fixed amount of land which may be bought and sold. It is different because over the years, in almost every single year the farmer on the land has received a lower income than have other Canadians generally. On the basis of net income agriculture has long been a depressed industry. If you do not provide some form of long-term credit to this underpaid industry you are going to see the growth of corporation farms, and you are going to see a great many farmers pushed off the land.
I want to agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Greenwood when he said that apparently the board had been conducting its policy over the years generally from a profit standpoint, and that its business was being carried out more from the standpoint of making at least some profit for the corporation than from a public service standpoint. Before the bill was taken to the committee
7.	1956	3631
Canadian Farm Loan Act we heard in the house the criticism that the board and its appraisers had generally been too cautious in making appraisals, and that the length of time taken to process an application was much too long. I do not know whether the parliamentary assistant will agree when I say that it seems to me that ample evidence was brought forward in the committee to substantiate those statements to the effect that the board was too cautious in its lending policy and that its appraisals took an undue length of time.
It is essential that farmers have access to long-term mortgage credit at reasonable rates of interest. It is essential not only from the standpoint of maintaining family farm units as distinct from corporation farms, but it is also necessary if we are to save prospective purchasers of land from paying exceedingly high rates of interest. I take it that by this act we want to provide money to prospective purchasers at 5 per cent interest rather than force them to seek loans at what are bound to be much higher rates of interest. We have had ample evidence before the committee, in discussing another measure, to show that even persons who operate businesses with a very high net worth sometimes must pay mortgage rates of interest of from 8 per cent to 15 per cent. Unless we provide mortgage money to prospective land purchasers at a reasonable rate of interest we are going to turn over the purchase of farms and the credit entailed therein to loan sharks and persons charging phenomenal rates of interest.
I suggest that the future attitude of the board should be one of seeking business, looking to do a job for agriculture, and not being so overly cautious as it has been in the past and not taking nearly so long in processing applications for loans. There have been a number of suggestions by members of this group as to how the present legislation should be improved.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, having noted what you have just said I shall be very brief in my comments at this time. At the outset

I would also like to pay tribute to Dr. Hope for the help he gave the committee in its consideration of this bill. He gave us a great deal of valuable information, and did not hesitate to give us the time we required of him. The evidence we received from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and from the briefs of other farm organizations showed quite clearly that the farm loan board perhaps have been overconservative in the appraisals they have made, and also perhaps have been taking a little too long in executing the loans. When we had the chairman of the farm loan board under examination we felt that, as a result of the answers he gave us, the charges that had been made by those organizations were well-founded.
I want to make it clear that we in this group are not at all keen in trying to get the farmers farther into debt; far from it. We would be quite happy if the farmers could continue without having to borrow from any farm loan board or from any other organization but unfortunately, owing to the government's present farm policy or perhaps I should say lack of farm policy, the majority of the farmers are being driven into debt whether they like it or not. However, they have to go into debt or quit farming. Since we have the position where, in order to continue, the farmers have to go into debt, then I think we have a duty to see to it that they have the best kind of credit available to them as far as the type of payment and cost are concerned.
Apparently the three main reasons why farmers today are pleading for loans under the farm loan board legislation is that first of all many of them are trying to expand their land holdings. Some may ask, "Is that wise?" Farmers have not very much choice. They are in a cost-price squeeze, and no matter how much they may try to reduce their costs there is a certain overhead that they cannot reduce. Therefore the only way they can reduce the impact of their overhead is to expand the size of their operation so that the cost per bushel or unit will be that much less.
We have had evidence in the past to show that the economic unit for a grain farm is around two sections of general land or one section of really good land. We have many farmers who are trying to operate on a half section or a three-quarter section basis. A farm of that size cannot support the cost of a full line of machinery. Therefore the farmer appeals to the farm loan board to get a mortgage in order to try to add to his land holdings and in that way reduce the impact of the overhead.
Then today we have many sons wishing to tske over the farms of their fathers. The
Canadian Farm Loan Act fathers need cash for their farms in order to retire, so the sons endeavour to get mortgages from the farm loan board to buy the farms from the fathers. Another rather unfortunate reason is that some of the farmers have obtained loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act and are not able to meet their payments today. Because of that they try to get a loan from the farm loan board in order to amortize the amount of the payment to the farm loan people over a long period of time, because loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act are made for machinery and only for a 3-year period. That means that in many instances the size of the payment is far beyond their ability to pay today. Therefore we feel that the farm loan board can perform a useful service. It has performed a useful service for many farmers, but we feel those services are probably going to be required, unfortunately, to a far greater extent in the future than they have been required in the past. Since this bill will undoubtedly bring about a number of improvements we intend to support it.

Clause 6, however, is quite broad; therefore I feel that any remarks I might have made on the first clause can be made here. I want to express my personal appreciation to all those who presented briefs before the banking and commerce committee. These briefs were most helpful, especially the brief presented by Mr. Brodrick of the federation of agriculture. Later we had Dr. Hope as a witness before the committee and he was very helpful indeed. We appreciate the fact that the government has brought in one or two amendments to the act. There was also one amendment made by the standing committee. However, we believe there are many changes that could be made so far as the administration of the act is concerned.
One very important thing, and it has been mentioned before, is the speeding up of appraisals and the processing of applications. In its brief the federation of agriculture suggested that there should be an advisory committee in each county. During the hearings of the committee I suggested that it would often be possible to use the services of some retired farmer in the district who knew the county very well and could be paid so much for each appraisal he was called upon to make. It would not be necessary for him to go into all the details in getting information that a stranger coming to the area would
require to obtain, and these local people would be invaluable in speeding up the processing of loans.
From questioning the chairman of the board it was learned that apparently some such individuals are used, but there are still a great number of permanent employees going around the country making appraisals. I suggest sincerely that the board give the most serious consideration to trying to get a good local farmer, retired or otherwise, in those districts where no local man is being used to do appraising at the present time. These men know the local situation and would be of very great help to the board in valuation and appraisal work.
It has been mentioned by the hon. member for Peterborough that there are hundreds of these applications that members of parliament do not see because they are personal matters. A person making such an application does not always like to come to his member about it unless he has trouble. If he has trouble then he probably will go to his member of parliament and in that case we do hear about these cases. I know that so far as any cases I have had to do with are concerned, the appraisal value has in most instances been very low compared with the actual value of the farm. The chairman of the board said they appraise a farm on the basis of its earning capacity.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Productive capacity.

speechtext:
That is probably a good idea,, but if that is the case then they are actually making loans on the basis of the person rather than the farm, because if a poor farmer was operating the best farm in the world the earning capacity of that farm would be very low. Therefore what they are doing in effect is lending money on the basis of the owner of the farm instead of on the farm. At the present time the situation is, as has been said, that farmers are in a low category so far as earnings are concerned. Their earnings are the lowest they have been for years. Ordinarily I suppose a farm would be remortgaged about every 20 or 25 years. Many farmers want to obtain one of these loans to consolidate their debts. They are probably paying off debts to the implement company or the bank and they want to consolidate them in one place where they will have a reasonable interest rate.
I always understood that the farm loan-board was supposed to be a service organization for the farmers, and that its purpose was to take up the slack in mortgage money when trust companies and private individuals who would ordinarily lend money were-making fewer and fewer loans. It was my

Canadian Farm Loan Act understanding that the purpose of the board was to be of service to people who found it difficult to get loans from any other source. But we find that the board had a profit of practically $163,000 last year and paid income tax amounting to $73,341. While it is to be hoped that the board will be able to pay expenses and make some profit, it seems to me to be a little out of the ordinary that the board should make that much profit on its operations.
. ' Take the case of the young man who wants to start farming. It is very odd that when he goes to the farm loan board and tries to get a loan he cannot get sufficient money in order to start farming unless he has a considerable amount of his own or unless his father turns the farm over to him free of cost. Ordinarily the farmer depends on the money he gets from his farm in order to retire, but the present situation means that he cannot retire. He must remain on the farm and either hire his son as a labourer or else operate on a share basis with him. It seems to me that if the young man wants to make farming his life work it should be a little easier for him to do so. The board should make it possible for him to start farming on a reasonable amount of capital and at the same time allow the father to retire, move off the farm and leave it to the son to run.
We all know that father-son arrangements sometimes create difficulty. The young man has new ideas and wants to carry on in a little different way than his father did. The father of course is sometimes just a little reluctant to do that. Such a situation often means that the boy leaves the farm because he does not have the amount of capital required.
The strange thing is that the same boy can go to the city, get a job and, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, have a new home built for him in the city for 10 per cent of the cost of the house. But if he goes into farming he has to have 60 per cent to 75 per cent of the value of the operation; that is, machinery, livestock, the value of the farm. He would probably have to have 60 per cent to 70 per cent of the amount of money he would require to start farming. He certainly cannot get credit on livestock. He cannot get very much credit on implements. Up to now you have only allowed him a loan of 60 per cent of the appraised value, and under the amendment it will be 65 per cent.
I suugest most sincerely that the appraised value is low, and that a loan of 65 per cent of the appraised value is a pretty poor show so far as the young man is concerned who
	I

is starting in the business of farming. As I said at the outset, I think most people appreciate the amendments that have been brought forward, but they do not go far enough. In the committee we tried to get 75 per cent of the appraised value established as the basis for a loan. That was turned down by the majority of the committee, but I suggest that it has to be either the one thing or the other. There either has to be an easing so far as appraisals are concerned or the percentage of the present appraisals should be increased.
If the farm loan board appraisers will ease up on their appraisals and appraise farms closer to their actual value at the present time, then 65 per cent might be sufficient. But it is either one thing or the other. If they are going to maintain the inadequate appraisal values they are using now, then I say the percentage should be increased.
It was suggested that the maximum loan be raised from $15,000 to $20,000. Even $20,000 on a large operation would not set a young farmer up in business. The maximum loans as originally provided was $10,000 on the first mortgage and $3,000 on the second. This amount has been increased to $15,000. That is a step in the right direction. But with values increasing in the way they are increasing at the present time, I personally feel-as do our party-that $15,000 is not enough for the maximum.
We are glad the government saw fit to increase the number of years from 25 to 30. I am sure that is a good move. As I said at the outset, ordinarily farmers remortgage, generally speaking, every 20 or 25 years. It naturally follows that the farm must be remortgaged when a son takes over, unless the farmer is wealthy enough so that he can turn over the farm to his son without compensation. As I say, it naturally follows that it must be remortgaged. Ordinarily a farmer wants to retire at somewhere about the age of 55 or 60, if he can do so. I suggest it is almost necessary that he retire at that age unless he wants to hold his son on the farm until he is 35 or 40 years of age before he is able to take that farm over. I think that is rather bad policy, as a rule, if it can be arranged in any other way. I think 30 years is a very good limit. Certainly the maximum should be increased under present conditions. I hope there is some way in which the government can see fit to do that.
As to the percentage, I hope the farm loan board will take into consideration getting a good local farmer in each county to help them with the appraisal of these farms, and to give them the information which they would necessarily be obliged to go out and dig for if

they did not have a local man. The suggestion made by the federation of agriculture is perfectly all right; I refer to the suggestion with regard to having an advisory committee. Under that suggestion you would have three when, in my opinion, one would probably be sufficient. As I said before, this legislation is acceptable. We intend to support the bill. However, we should like to see these various changes made.

speechtext:
I am interested in clause 6, especially subsection (i) with reference to loans of up to 65 per cent on the actual value of such lands and buildings. I am interested because the provision does not mean a thing as far as my part of the country is concerned, where the average farmer makes his living from fruit trees. I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant later on to define the policy the department has in valuing mature fruit trees.
I get from my riding constant evidence that the present system of valuation is entirely wrong, that it has no relation to actual value. If future loans are to be made on the basis of 65 per cent of the actual value, I think it is time the government had in the interior someone competent to value fruit trees. I am satisfied that at the present time they are not properly valued, and that they are definitely valued at only a fraction of the value of such fruit lands on the open market.
Actually, some time ago I had instances of two fruit farmers who were turned down by the farm loan board on the basis of the valuation of their fruit trees, but in both cases they were able to go, with the same security, to an orthodox chartered bank and arrange a loan, at probably the same rates of interest. I do not know the rates of interest, but they were able to satisfy the orthodox bank that they were capable of meeting the payments on the loan. There is something wrong when this happens with a board which is supposed to assist in getting out of a bad spot those who normally cannot get their assistance from the banks; that is, if they are a fairly good risk otherwise.
As far as we in British Columbia are concerned, I think having the operations of the farm loan board concentrated in New Westminster is wrong. That is on the coast, where the climate is totally different and where growing conditions are different. They have nothing to speak of in the way of fruit trees. We should have one of these people situated in the interior-in the Okanagan valley or the Kootenay valley-in order to become acquainted with fruit growing conditions and with the value of growing fruit trees in order that a fair assessment can be made. Even with the 65 per cent provision I am satisfied 67509-231
Canadian Farm Loan Act that on these appraisals the average fruit grower could get only half that on the market value of his 10 acres or maybe 15 acres of fruit land.
These are the questions I should like to pose to the parliamentary assistant. What definitely is the policy of the government in valuing fruit trees? I just want to support what has been said by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary because we have similar experience particularly in connection with the fruit industry. I represent a number of fruit farmers and small mixed farmers, the great majority of them with a long record of successful operation of small acreages compared to the giant farms looked after by my colleagues around me.
They have managed with remarkably few mortgages. I mention that fact to indicate the soundness of their small farming operations. They have few mortgages indeed. For some years I have not seen a single farm in my constituency advertised as delinquent with regard to taxes. I mention that fact to indicate that these are good farmers and that they are engaged in good, sound farming propositions. They run their farms mostly with family labour. They have not much equipment. They are more acquainted with the cross-cut saw, the axe, the walking plow and the mattock than they are with large machinery requiring large investment. Their operations are modest. You will not find them in California, in Arizona or at the Empress hotel in Victoria. They are obliged to stay home all winter in order to attend to their pruning and things of that sort.
As I say. there is a tendency to underestimate the production value of these small orchards. Like the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary, I should like the parliamentary assistant to explain to the committee on what formula they operate with respect to the valuation of fruit farms particularly.
As I mentioned at the resolution stage, I believe it was, I am of the opinion that the activities of the board should be diversified. At present they are centralized in New Westminster, and as far as I can see they are hypnotized by Fraser valley conditions. They know little from experience of Okanagan and

I would seriously suggest again that the officials of the board would be well advised to get in touch with the farmers' organizations, to visit the fruit growers' organizations and to get an abstract from the books in order to see what has been the production of some of these people.
