speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this clause proved to be the most contentious one before the banking and commerce committee. It deals with the basis upon which loans are made. There seems to be a considerable variation in the policies followed by the appraisers of the Canadian farm loan board. Experience has been that anyone attempting to get a loan from the board finds that the value put upon his property by the

appraiser is significantly less than the current resale value of his farm.
Another aspect of the problem was discussed under an earlier clause. The Canadian farm loan board operates upon the difference between the cost for which they can borrow money and the interest rate they charge the farmer. One way they can make certain that no risk will be involved is to be very conservative in their appraisal policy. Section 6 (1) (a) reads in part:
-the principal amount of which shall not exceed sixty-five per cent of the actual value of such land-
The term "actual value" is very vague indeed. It has been claimed that it is based upon the productivity of the land, but in order to have a valuation based upon productivity you must give consideration to the market prices of the products which are produced. I think in the final analysis the actual value should be based on the longterm productivity of the land.
It is evident from the experience of many farmers that the actual value placed on a piece of land by the appraisers of the Canadian farm loan board is significantly less than the appraisal of the actual value of a piece of land by the Department of National Revenue for succession duty purposes. There should be some consistency in the policies. In one case we have the Department of National Revenue putting the highest possible valuation on a piece of land for succession duty purposes, and then we have the farm Joan board apparently determined to put a very low value on a piece of land so a smaller loan may be made and the risk thereby reduced.
Considering the experience of other countries I do not think we need be as niggardly as the government has shown a desire to be in the percentage of the appraised value. The farmers' home administration and the farmers' credit administration in the United States grant loans on the basis of 100 per cent of the appraised value, and the losses have been small. There is a slight variation in the administration of those boards as compared with the Canadian administration, but I think our officials would do well to study those credit agencies in the United States.
It is generally thought that the government is increasing the percentage of the actual value by this new bill. Previously the percentage of the actual value was 60 per cent and it has been raised to 65 per cent, but I submit that percentage is deceptive. Prior to this amendment the board was taking 60 per cent on the first mortgage and then there was an additional $2,000 for the second mortgage. Under the present bill it is 65 per cent

of the actual value, so that when the two are correlated it will be seen that the percentage of the actual value has not been increased.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is aware of this problem and has advocated that the percentage of the actual value be increased to 80 per cent for loans up to $8,000. It is significant to note that the largest proportion of the loans made by the board are well under $8,000. In an effort to keep the legislation in line with the desires of the farm organizations in Canada who have made a complete appraisal of the situation, who have made a study of it and who have realized that the percentage of the actual value of the land upon which a loan is made is much too low, I take advantage of this opportunity to correct that situation by moving.
That clause 6 be amended by deleting the word "sixty-five" in line 19 and substituting the word "eighty" therefor.
If this amendment is adopted it will broaden the whole scope of the Canadian farm loan board so it may be able to fulfil more adequately its role as the primary credit agency in Canada, without being limited to the small loans which have been made in the past. By having a larger percentage of the appraised value upon which a loan can be made we will be in position to establish young farmers on economic units, since we will be allowing them sufficient money to permit them to become thoroughly established.
It will also give us an opportunity to keep the procedure of the Canadian farm loan board in pace with the continuing depreciation of the Canadian dollar. It must be recognized that as our dollar depreciates, land values increase. Land which sold for $30 an acre some years ago is now selling for $60 an acre. Unless the percentage of the appraised value is increased it will be virtually impossible for young farmers to get the money required to establish themselves on farm units.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make some comments on clause 6. I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Greenwood when he more or less philosophized on farming in general. He quoted some very fine words from equally quotable people. I quite agree with the sentiments he expressed.
I feel that what we should do is strike at the hard core of what this bill is proposing. The members of this group feel that we should be thankful for small mercies from this government, but we submit that the present bill as it is constituted, with the amendments that have been made thereto, does not meet the farm financing problem in this country. It falls far short of providing the kind of farm credit administration we need for farming generally in Canada.
I want to support the hon. member for Kindersley and other hon. members in what they have said. I think a new perspective is needed in Canada with respect to farm credit. It has been indicated that this clause which provides for a loan on the basis of 65 per cent of the appraised value of the land is not satisfactory. Anyone who is familiar with agriculture today will agree with that statement. I certainly agree with those who say today that a great extension of farm credit under conditions where farmers, particularly those in western Canada, are operating under a great disparity between their prices and costs and the returns they receive, could be a dangerous thing to the farm economy. However, when one recognizes that the farmer finds himself in a price-cost squeeze and that we have had increases in farm machinery costs and increases all along the line, it is readily recognized that something more adequate should be provided for the Canadian farmers if we are going to maintain and promote the family farm.
There are four objectives we should have in mind when we are thinking of farm credit. The first is the achievement of security of the family farm. Second, attention should be given to the extension of credit which will provide an economic farm unit. Third, the tenant farmer who is presently farming rented land, and who has in mind the final ownership of that land, also needs credit with which he can operate that farm as an economic unit, with the final hope of owning it. Then there is a fourth objective we should have in mind, and that is the father-son relationship, where the father perhaps has been farming over the
3644	HOUSE OF
Canadian Farm Loan Act years and wishes to turn over his farm to his son and have his farm become the property of that son. If the older farmer wants to retire and turn it over to his son, we need adequate credit so the son may readily get it and carry on in the footsteps of his father.
When we consider that the best this government has to offer in the way of farm credit on a 5 per cent long-term basis, one can readily see that under present conditions, when we have had already this bill to extend farm credit, it could be very dangerous to the farm economy, because everyone recognizes that farming is a hazardous occupation and that the farmer has his economic ups and downs.
I am suggesting, while at the same time we should have long-term credit, that the first problem, of course, is to guarantee fair prices to the farmer. I am not going to enlarge upon that, but I should like to bring to the attention of this committee what is done in the United States, the great capitalist country to the south. Whilst I seldom recommend any of the economic policies of that country for this country, I think this government should at least look across the border and see what is being done in many ways to help the farmer there.
The agricultural attache here was kind enough to send me certain information in respect to broad policies undertaken with regard to farm credit in the United States. I should like to draw to the committee's attention one important aspect of assisting and financing agriculture in the United States. I have reference to the rural electrification program of the United States, under which over 4,468,000 farms have been electrified. Their interest under that program, which is repayable over a 35-year period, is not 5 per cent or 3J per cent, such as we have under V.L.A. in this country. The interest rate is 2 per cent; but this government is bringing in legislation, when farmers from one end of the country to the other are in the worst financial difficulties they have ever been in, to offer us nothing better than a 5 per cent long-term program for farm credit.
So I say this bill is completely inadequate, t am suggesting, first, along with the hon. member for Kindersley and others, that the term of credit should be extended from 25 years to 40 years. As was pointed out in the committee of the house which made an investigation into farm credit, if the extension of credit were amortized over a period of 40 years instead of 25 years it would reduce the interest rate payable on an amortized basis so the farmer would in effect be paying less interest than he does under


the short-term amortization period. So I am suggesting, if we pass this bill this year, that next year this government take a good hard look at farm credit in this country.
I feel that farming today is in great jeopardy. It is once again hitting the kind of depression we had in the 1930's; and it seems hard, for those of us in close touch with the agricultural picture in this country, to place before this government enough information so it will take seriously the problem facing the farmer today. So I just want to point out that this bill today, as amended, falls far short of the kind of farm credit we should have in this country. The farmers' union, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and all the great farm bodies have indicated to the government that something more far-reaching than this bill should have been presented to the house at this time. It seems to me that this bill, which was framed many years ago, has been overhauled from time to time, but there has been very little indication that the government has any knowledge of the kind of credit we need for farmers today.
Before sitting down I wish to re-emphasize that the picture I have obtained by surveying the financial situation throughout my constituency-and I think it is comparable to many, particularly on the prairies-is that this is not going to meet the problem. This is nothing more than putting a millstone around the necks of many farmers. Today they cannot sell their grain, and they cannot meet the price-cost squeeze. They will be forced to get bank credit at 5 per cent amortized over 20 years. In effect this will be a millstone around their necks for many years. Rather than having something adequate given to this house, a bill that would play fair with the farmer, one by which the farmer would be able to liquidate his debts, become the full owner of his farm and be able to farm an economic unit on a family basis, we may go back to the corporation farm and more and more see the family unit farm go off the Canadian scene.
In closing I may say that I think the government has been remiss in its duties when it cannot see any way of extending, through the Bank of Canada or otherwise, low interest rates to our farmers. Sometimes we hear it said that the farmers are subsidized. The reason the farmer today needs the kind of credit I am suggesting is the very fact that the farmer, in paying the high prices for farm machinery and other costs, is in effect subsidizing General Motors and the farm machinery companies because he is paying their profits. For example, when General Motors can make over a billion dollars profit

this year, when Canada Packers are able to rebuild complete plants in four years, I say the farmer is subsidizing many industries in this country, and it is not the farmer who is being subsidized.

No, Mr. Chairman. The bill as it was sent to the banking and commerce committee provided for a maximum loan period of 25 years. Members who were on that committee will recall that an amendment was moved and accepted by the committee changing the period from 25 to 30 years. At that time some of us expressed the hope that the committee would go one step farther and provide a maximum amortization period of 40 years. If that had been done we would have followed the recommendation made to the committee by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
I believe there are good reasons why the committee of the whole should consider extending the maximum period for farm mortgages. A 25-year period with an interest rate of 5 per cent establishes a repayment rate of 7-25 per cent. That rate, with farm income as it usually is established, is a relatively high rate. Extending the period to
Canadian Farm Loan Act 30 years will reduce the 7-25 per cent to something under 7 per cent. But if we extended the maximum period to 40 years, even assuming the maximum interest rate were left at 5 per cent, the repayment rate would be reduced to 5-83 per cent. I suggest that a repayment rate of 5-83 per cent is more in keeping with the actual rate that agriculture can bear than the rate of over 7 per cent brought about by the bill.
I was very interested in the committee to hear Dr. Hope relate to us on this point the results of a survey made of the length of term of farm mortgages in Ontario. He gave us this breakdown. Eight per cent of the farms in Ontario were mortgaged for a period in excess of 50 years. Fourteen per cent of the farms were mortgaged for a period of 41 to 48 years. Fourteen per cent of the farms were mortgaged for a period of 33 to 40 years. Seventeen per cent were mortgaged for a period of 25 to 32 years, 16 per cent for a period of 17 to 24 years, 13 per cent for a period of 9 to 16 years, 12 per cent for a period of 1 to 8 years, and 6 per cent had no mortgage at all.
Therefore, according to his sample survey a majority of the farms in Ontario were mortgaged for a period of 25 years or more; to be exact, 53 per cent. We were given this further information by way of breaking down mortgage capital and its source. Fifty per cent of the mortgages were held by individuals other than the seller. Thirty-three per cent of the mortgages were held by the seller. Nine per cent were held by loan companies, 4 per cent were family mortgages and only 3 per cent were mortgages from government agencies, with 1 per cent listed as being under the Veterans' Land Act. Therefore the total mortgage business done in Ontario by government institutions, of which the Canadian farm loan board is certainly the main one, is approximately 3 per cent.
That fact, Mr. Chairman, together with the fact brought out in the survey that 53 per cent of the farms in Ontario carry mortgages for periods in excess of 25 years, suggests to me that the burden of mortgages that must be paid for and serviced by agriculture is indeed high and that the committee should give sympathetic consideration to any improvement that can be made in the bill before us. Therefore I suggest that the maximum period of repayment should be increased from 30 years, as provided in the amendment, to a period of 40 years. I do so with the full support of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and with the full support of authorities who have looked into the field of farm mortgage credit very carefully. As far as I know, no authority has recommended a maximum

Canadian Farm. Loan Act period of less than 30 years, and some authorities have recommended periods even in excess of 40 years. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I move:
That clause 6 be amended by deleting the word "thirty" in line 35 and substituting the word "forty" therefor.

Mr. Chairman, I think there is a very good reason why a terrfi of 40 years should be provided in the law rather than 30 years. That is the fact, and it is a fact, that it is impossible for farmers generally to meet a high rate of interest on mortgages. The history of mortgage repayments bears that out. Dr. Hope's evidence has been referred to in a very favourable way by members of

all parties, and in my opinion he showed conclusively that a long repayment period is necessary.
Some of us have endeavoured to get the mortgage rate of interest reduced by getting the government to accept the carrying and administrative costs of the board. We have not done that because we believe the government should subsidize everything but because we believe a total interest rate of 5 per cent is probably all that agriculture can bear over a long period of time. Even if we provide a mortgage period of 40 years, the effective repayment rate will still remain at 5-83 per cent. A 30-year mortgage is a long mortgage, perhaps, for a private business; I do not know. It may be a long mortgage for a corporation. It may be a long mortgage for individuals other than farmers. But I suggest that in the history of agricultural credit a mortgage term of 40 years over which repayment is to be made is not too long when you consider that any shorter period will increase the repayment rate.
To support my contention that a 5 per cent rate over a 40-year period is the maximum that agriculture generally can support, I should like to refer to the evidence given by Dr. Hope showing the return to the farm operator and for farm family labour over a period of 29 years, from 1926 to 1954, in Canada. Those figures show that the average return to the operator for his labour and management over this 29-year period is less than $1,000 a year; in fact it is just $967, and you may add to that the return to the farm operator for his management and the wages of his unpaid family help, namely another $219, bringing an average total net income to the farm operator and his family of $1,186 a year over a period of 29 years.
With that history of agriculture before us, I think it is fair to say that a rate of 5-83 per cent is the very maximum rate that agriculture generally can bear. I therefore believe the suggestion that the maximum amortization period should be 40 years deserves support by the committee. I would point out to the hon. member for Greenwood something that is obvious, namely that anybody who can repay in 30 years or a shorter period of time has that right. But I am making this plea for a longer period so that many farm operators who must have a longer period in which to repay and a smaller rate of repayment may have this further assistance.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it would be of interest to the committee to have some information as to the experience of the board in their 25 years of operation in so far

as the actual need for longer terms is concerned. I am informed that while most contracts are entered into for the maximum term, which has been 25 years and now will be 30 years, the rate of prepayment of loans is such that the average term over the 25-year period is only 14 years.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to take any part in this debate, but as time has gone on the spirit has moved me to do so. We hear talk about a 40-year term for a mortgage. My friends have mortgages which run for 10-year or 12-year periods. Forty years is the working life of any farmer. A fellow goes on a farm at 25 years of age. That is about as soon as he will get on a farm of his own. With this suggested provision it is going to bring him to the age of 65 or 70 before the mortgage is paid off, or he may die with the mortgage still hanging over the farm. That is like the fellow who lives on the farm all his life and leaves it to his son with a greater mortgage against it than it is worth.
I agree with the hon. member who said that probably the interest rate could be reduced to 4 per cent or 4J per cent. I think everybody would be pleased about that, even the fellow who is buying the mortgage. As to the 40-year period, I cannot agree with the suggestion at all. If a man cannot see some daylight, or if he does not see some time ahead when he is going to have the mortgage paid off within his lifetime, I think it would be poor business for the farmer who is borrowing the money and also for the government that is lending it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am interested to hear our friends in the Conservative party disagreeing with the Canadian Federation of Agriculture so pointedly. One of the specific recommendations of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is that the amortization period be 40 years. In presenting evidence before the committee they indicated that this was necessary in order-as the hon. member for Assiniboia has pointed out-to reduce the annual payment that must be made. I think anyone who is really concerned about the welfare of agriculture will support the amendment he has moved because, as was pointed out, there are no flexible terms of repayment in the present act-something which the federation is also advocating-so the amount you would repay annually would have some relationship to the productivity to the farm in that particular area. Correspondingly, if there were an extremely low return from the farm, the repayment would be lessened.
By increasing the period of repayment we give to the farmer a greater opportunity to repay the money he has borrowed. He will
Canadian Farm Loan Act therefore have a greater amount of capital with which to keep his farm operating. I think we cannot assume that a farmer must be any different to those in a great many other businesses. I believe you will find many businessmen who are 40 years of age or 50 years of age who might happen to borrow $20,000 or $30,000. I do not believe we expect them to have that loan fully repaid in their lifetime, and I do not think it is a terrific burden on them. But in the case of agricultural land which has a significant mortgage-holding capacity, the better the terms of repayment we can give, the better chance agriculture will have to equate itself with the other occupations in Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I might say that we intend to support the amendment, because by increasing the period to 40 years we shall, of course, reduce the amount of the annual payment. The parliamentary assistant referred to the fact that during the past 25 years there has been prepayment, bringing that term down to 14 years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

speechtext: On the average.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: But the parliamentary assistant must remember that during that period we had a war, which was an inflationary period, followed by another inflationary period; and it is always far easier to pay off debts during a period of inflation than it is during a period of deflation. At the present time we have a situation where net farm income has dropped by 40 per cent in the past five years. If the situation we have today continues I would say that the farmers will not be able to pay their mortgage off in 40 years, let alone in 25 years. I think probably the best thing we can do is to support the amendment to increase the period to 40 years, in order to get the annual payment down to as low a figure as possible.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be few. It seems to me that we very easily could have gone along with a new type of valuation program which would have placed the farmer in a position to make a purchase with a smaller down payment. In that respect I think we might have brought this legislation more in line with the National Housing Act. In providing monthly payments I believe we have set up a program here that will bring within the reach of more people the orderly payment of their indebtedness. But no matter what type of business is involved, if we are going along with the system as we have it now it seems to me that we have to leave some pride in ownership and the acquisition of ownership. If there is not a sense of responsibility left in connection with those things which we attempt to acquire,

Canadian Farm Loan Act we might as well have the government buy all the property and lease it out on a 40-year basis to whomever wants to work it. If ownership means anything, therefore, you have to put something into it. If we are going to provide a period of time so long that in the ordinary course of events many of the people who will be living on these properties will not have paid for them by the time they die, then I think that sense of responsibility will disappear and the country will be the worse for it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
I did not intend to say anything about this, but since the amendment has come up I wish to say a few words. I have had the opportunity of living in a rural community in which the farmers need loans and apply for them. I think we should be consistent. In requesting the 40-year term I believe the federation of agriculture also had in mind increasing the amount of the loan to $20,000 and the amount of the appraised value from 75 per cent to 80 per cent.
Since we are not going to get an increase in the valuation of the property beyond 65 per cent-I am sorry about that because I feel the government could very well have brought that up to 75 per cent-and since the total amount of the loan is not to go beyond $15,000, I think we must be consistent and say that a 30-year term is a fair term on which to make that loan. A good many of the people to whom I have had the opportunity of speaking thought a term of 30 years or even 25 years would be quite satisfactory, provided they could get an increase in the appraised value. They would rather have had an increase in the appraised value. For these reasons I cannot support the amendment.

I should like to point out, Mr. Chairman, in support of the argument that has been advanced for the 40-year period, that it amounts to about this. In the case of the 40 years the payments are less. If agricultural conditions are good, the farmer will be able to repay his loan and be clear of it. If agricultural conditions are bad, then what is going to happen if he does not pay within the 30 years? He is put off the farm. If hon. members to the right look at their argument they will find they are really jeopardizing the farmer, because the whole thing depends upon the agricultural conditions which exist during that period.
The parliamentary assistant has already pointed out that experience shows that even if the period of repayment is 25 years, when farmers are in a position to pay they prepay and get rid of the debt. By extending the period of time you are reducing the likelihood of a foreclosure. It gives the farmer an extra 10 years of grace. As we know from experience in Canada, agricultural conditions change rapidly and on numerous occasions the period of bad times in agriculture has extended over a long period of time. This extra 10 years merely affords these farmers a safeguard and lessens the likelihood of a foreclosure because of inability to pay.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: I have taken the opportunity of making the calculation and perhaps the parliamentary assistant would verify the figures. It is not a one-way street. If a man borrows $100 for 40 years instead of 30 years, in the 40 years he pays back $233.20 for the $100 he borrowed as against $195.30 that he would pay back in 30 years. In other words there is a difference of $37.90.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: I am amazed at the position of the official opposition in this regard. I can understand the government, which has control of the public purse, feeling that it should look at this matter cautiously, carefully and in a conservative manner before agreeing to further extend the period when they have already extended the 25 years to 30 years.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REORGANIZE CAPITAL STRUCTURE, INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Don't you do that?

speechtext:
If the Conservatives are announcing tonight that they are going to be across the way after the next election, as the hon. member for Kamloops is suggesting, then I suggest that by their statements they are saying that so far as policy is concerned they are going to do exactly the same as the

government now in office. In this discussion the parliamentary assistant has been able to sit back rather contently and allow the members of the official opposition to advance arguments against the position taken by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Perhaps the 30 years, as the period of the loan under the Liberal government, would not be any different from 30 years under a Conservative government. The Conservatives say you should not extend the 30 years to 40 because it would cost the farmer too much. Why then do they want to extend the 25 years to 30 years? Why did the hon. member for Greenwood try so hard-and I admired him for that-to be the person who would extend the 25 to 30, and hold his position for 10 minutes by beating down government members on an amendment which had been agreed to by the government? If the hon. member for St. Paul's had been coaching him, he could have pointed out that the farmer would save a lot more if the period had been 25 years instead of 30. As a matter of fact the farmer would save a lot if he did not have to get a loan at all. If the Conservatives followed their argument to its logical conclusion they would want to reduce the period even further.
Then the hon. member for Victoria-Car-leton said the federation of agriculture had three proposals. One was to increase the percentage of the appraised value; the second was to set the maximum loan above the 65 per cent and then he said they wanted the maximum loan to go beyond $15,000. The third proposal was to increase the 25 years to 40, and he said that depended on getting the other two, and that unless they got all three they were not going to support one of them. I suggest that even if the government has said no to an increase in the 65 per cent, as it has; even if the government has said no to an increase in the maximum amount of the loan, that is no reason why we should not at this time attempt to get an increase in the period of repayment.
The rate of repayment, as has been pointed out, for a 30-year period is $6.51. The rate of repayment for a 40-year period is $5.83. Someone may say there is not too much difference between these figures, a difference of some three-quarters of 1 per cent; but I suggest' to the members of the committee that in a period like the present, when farm income is so low, there is a great deal of difference between $5.83 and $6.51, and that farmers will have real difficulty in meeting even $5.83 and, of course, even more difficulty in paying $6.51. All of us would like to see farm mortgages kept in practice to as short a period as possible; all of us would like to see farmers in the position where they would be able to 67509-232J
Canadian Farm Loan Act pay their mortgages in a short time. But we should not penalize the farmer by keeping the period at 30 years if there is any possible chance of getting the maximum period extended to 40 years.
Someone has said we would be keeping the mortgage on the farm until the farmer is 70 years of age. Well, that is nothing new; and any change we make in this legislation is not likely to change the position in Ontario, the statistics of which I referred to a moment ago.
I do not think it is necessarily a question of a given farmer taking out a mortgage and himself repaying it. That is desirable, but I do not think it is essential. We have a National Housing Act. Some of the mortgages are a very high percentage of the sale value. I have never had the privilege of buying a house, but I am told by those people who buy houses and by people who sell them from time to time that you have a much better chance to sell a city house at a reasonable price if there is a substantial mortgage against it and therefore the cash payment is low.
I suggest that a farmer is more likely to sell his farm with ease at a fair market price if the down payment is not too high. If a man on reaching the age of 70 has a farm with a Canadian farm loan board mortgage on it which has not reached the period of 40 years and he decides to sell the farm, I suggest that he will dispose of his property more easily if there is a mortgage on it at a reasonable rate of interest and the cash payment to obtain the farm is therefore lower than if there were no mortgage against it and the farmer had to demand full cash when he sold the farm. Therefore I suggest we should not compare the 40-year term with the normal productivity of a farm. That is not too material. I think it is good business that agricultural mortgages generally should carry a low rate of repayment.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to say anything about this bill at all, but I think our friends to the left are being very pessimistic. I suggest that by saying what he has just said the hon. member for Assiniboia is being so pessimistic that he thinks farming is not going to be any better in the next several years. I suggest to him that our policy would make farming so much better that we would not need any legislation like this.

Mr. Chairman, the minister when introducing this legislation, gave quite a lengthy outline of its purposes, which is contained in Hansard of March 8, commencing at page 1921, and I do not think any further explanation is required in a general way.
This bill now comes to the house after having been considered by the banking and commerce committee, which had the benefit of hearing, among other witnesses, the president and also the general manager of the bank. I think an attempt was made there to try to eliminate discussions that did not have particular reference to this bill and might go a little further afield on to general monetary and banking policy. The reason was that it was known in the banking and commerce committee that the president of the bank in his capacity as governor of the Bank of Canada would, within a few days, be again appearing before the banking and commerce committee to discuss the Bank of Canada report. I would hope, Mr. Chairman, that on the same basis, difficult sometimes as it may be, it would appeal to the judgment of the committee similarly to try to keep the discussion to the industrial development bank amending bill rather than have a general discussion of monetary policy.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ENLARGE CLASSES OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the parliamentary assistant has said, this bill was discussed at length by the committee and I shall be very brief in the remarks I shall make. But I think it might perhaps be of some use to those here present who were not on the committee if I were to make one or two general observations as to the purport of this amending bill.
[The Deputy Chairman.]

In the main the amending bill does two things. It extends the scope of "industrial enterprise" or "industrial business" and it alters the proportion of the lending funds of the bank which may be used for loans of $200,000 and over. It does not increase the total amount the bank may lend, which depends upon the capital and reserve of the bank.
I would remind hon. members that the industrial development bank was designed really to fill a gap in our financial structure. A loan may be required for a longer term than a bank may be prepared to give it, yet it may not be large enough to warrant a bond issue in the ordinary course. You have thus an in-between situation which is filled by the industrial development bank, I think to the satisfaction of virtually all concerned. Although there was some misgiving on one point which I shall come to later, the banks have found that the industrial development bank fitted into the pattern of the financial structure of the country. One satisfactory aspect of the operations of the industrial development bank is that it has kept in close touch, and I think in useful touch, with the chartered banks.
I would point out the safeguards that exist. The bank is given the power to deal only with certain things. Those of us who had the advantage of hearing the governor of the bank I am sure will feel that it has remained in the area it was intended to cover. The impression we got from him was that he was content and did not wish to step outside. The governor put aside certain suggestions for expanding the operations of the bank, saying they were organized and equipped to scrutinize and deal with industrial enterprises, that that was really the scope of their operations and they should not extend it.
One of the questions he was asked was in connection with the provision that a loan may not be granted by the industrial development bank unless evidence is given that it has not been possible to obtain it elsewhere on reasonable terms. We asked him if that provision was taken seriously or treated in a routine manner, and he said it was far from routine. He told us that in a great many cases the industrial development bank would be in actual touch with other institutions from which loans had been requested, such as the chartered banks, and therefore the borrower had the advantage of having discussed the matter with both agencies.
The important point of this bill is to raise the amount which may be lent out in loans of $200,000 or more. Originally that was put at $25 million, it was raised to $50 million and it is now proposed to raise it to $75 million. The actual amount now outstanding

in loans of $200,000 or over is substantially less than $50 million. When we asked the governor why he wanted this substantial ex-tention he said that they were doing a job and they might as well do an adequate job. He said it seemed worth while to get a substantial further authorization.
Having regard to the fact that the bank was established originally to fill a gap, to do what the chartered banks were not completely organized to do, I was reassured to find that while the bank has played a useful part there has been no wild attempt to rush out for business. Indeed I would say that the bank has pursued the even tenor of its way. As far as I am concerned I think that is what it was intended to do. I think anyone who needs a loan of this kind can easily get in touch with the bank and get whatever accommodation he is entitled to.
There was one answer made by the governor of the bank I was interested in. When speaking about large loans he said that the largest loan made was for $4 million, which was much larger than any other loan. He said that there had been only three or four other loans as high as $1 million. The $4 million loan was made in special circumstances to a defence industry because of the type of work it was called upon to do.

I mention that because there may be others who like myself did not want to feel that this organization was trying to rock the boat by entering into competition with the chartered banks and other financial institutions.
Another point I had in my mind when this bill was announced was that it might be in effect going contrary to the restrictive credit measures we have been told about, that to some extent this would be going in the opposite direction. The question was whether this implied in effect a substantial creation of new money. Was it going contrary to the other things that were being done? I think the governor replied to the questions in that connection quite satisfactorily. When we asked if money loaned in this way would mean the creation of new money, while in a sense he said yes it could be, in the same breath he said that the bank by marketing methods could prevent a situation from actually resulting in the creation of new money.
But even more impressive than that, the feeling I got was that they were not going to be rushing out to make a number of large loans, that there was no intention of trying to change the bank from what it' had been into an organization which would try to spread

Industrial Development Bank Act itself all over the landscape. To sum up, I think one can fairly say that up to the present the bank has gone along the lines it was intended to follow, that it has been well run and has worked in harmony with the other agencies in the financial structure of this country. The main thing is that the new bill is not intended to increase the total amount which the bank will have available for lending but merely to increase the amount which may be lent in loans of $200,000 and more.
As I listened to the governor of the bank I felt that it had been conducted in a sensible fashion and that this was not going to be taken as an occasion to rush out and try to change the present character of the bank.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ENLARGE CLASSES OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we in this group, unlike the hon. member for Greenwood, would like to see the industrial development bank expand. We would like to see it stretch out. We would like to see it act aggressively in going after new business. We would like to see it do these things mainly because we would like to see new industries developed, and further because we would like to see new industries developed by Canadian capital.
We hear much about the desirability and the necessity of increasing the proportion of Canadian industries being developed by Canadian capital. Here is a bank, here is a Canadian enterprise in the business of promoting new Canadian industry with Canadian capital. I do not think the members of the official opposition are being completely consistent when they express the hope that the industrial development bank will not become aggressive, will not stretch out, will not expand at a rapid rate.
I repeat that I would like to see the industrial development bank use its authority and the money which is being made available to it by parliament in an aggressive way to establish new Canadian industries. I would like to see the industrial development bank come back to parliament in the near future for more funds; for the reason that it has in a short period of time successfully invested the funds it now has in new Canadian enterprises for the benefit of Canadians generally.
Looking over the annual report of the industrial development bank and the amount of business it has done in various provinces,
I cannot help being struck by the overwhelming preponderance of business that is done in the two central provinces as compared with the little amount of business being done, generally speaking, in the maritime and the prairie regions. I express the hope here that the industrial development bank will be successful in promoting new

Industrial Development Bank Act industries, not only all across Canada but to a greater extent, particularly, in the mari-times and on the prairies. I like to see Canada industrialized, but I like to see all parts of Canada share in that industrialization. To the extent that the industrial development bank can use its policies to allow Canadians in all provinces to share in that industrial development, I wish it great success.

If I might refer to those figures at the present time, the figures for authorizations to September 30, 1955, show that Ontario got some $29 million in authorizations, Manitoba just under $4 million, Saskatchewan just over $4 million, and Alberta somewhat under $7 million. If you take the single year 1955 and add up the figures for the three prairie provinces, you get some $l-4 million as compared with $5 * 5 million, or about one-quarter of the amount that was disbursed in Ontario. In other words, for the full period

the three prairie provinces combined obtained about half as much money as Ontario alone.
For the latest year, the three prairie provinces combined obtained approximately one-quarter of the amount obtained by Ontario. Then, as I am from Saskatchewan, the figure that naturally comes to my attention is the extremely low figure of $153,000 for that one-year period for Saskatchewan as compared with most of the other provinces.

include loans to hotel operators and hotel proprietors. Mr. Caswell went on to point out that the hotel industry was very essential to this nation; that hotel facilities in many, if not all, cities in Canada left much to be desired, and that adequate hotel accommodation would in fact improve the wealth of the nation by improving our tourist traffic.
Though I cannot refer to this at any length, we have just concluded the discussion of a loan policy for agriculture, and particularly a policy of making credit available for agriculture. The government has a policy, as defined in the Industrial Development Bank Act, to promote industries and new industrial development, and we are now discussing that policy. But there is an important section of our nation that is completely overlooked, I am afraid, as far as government policy is concerned. I refer to the ordinary independent businessman of this country. I refer to the hotelkeepers, the general merchants, the independent merchants whose services have meant so much to the country.
I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that the government should consider the extension of this act, and if that is not appropriate then the introduction of new legislation to provide for long-term credit at reasonable rates of interest to the ordinary independent merchant and businessman, the small businessman if you like, whose services are important to the nation and who at the moment, through no fault of his own, is unable to stand up against the ruthless competition of the big monopolies in these fields.
I do not know what other members may think, but I was certainly amazed to hear Mr. Caswell make the statement that the vast majority of hotel proprietors who wish to obtain new long-term mortgage capital to extend their businesses or for major renovations have in fact to pay a very substantial bonus on the capital they obtain. He told us of a personal experience he had when, in asking for a certain loan of $90,000 on a hotel, he was offered a mortgage with a face value of $117,000, in other words with a bonus attached of $27,000, together with an interest rate of 8 per cent. He did not have to take it because he was able to get his money elsewhere, but he was offered mortgage money at a rate of approximately 15 per cent a year. If that had been an isolated case one would not need to mention it, but Mr. Caswell told the banking and commerce committee that the majority of hotel proprietors in this country who want to obtain new capital to expand their businesses must pay a very heavy bonus when they obtain a mortgage, and that the final rate they pay is anywhere from 10 to 15 per cent per year.

Industrial Development Bank Act
I suggest that gives further impetus to the need for a new credit policy in this field in order to give the ordinary businessman something of a break and provide him with longterm credit at an interest rate that will more closely approach the interest rate at which the big chain stores and monopolies in the nation are able to obtain their credit. We in this group are pleased to support the measure. We hope the industrial development bank will be used to a much greater extent in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the members of the Social Credit group have studied this legislation both in the committee and outside the committee and we are in favour of it. We feel that it is only a small beginning in the direction of a much greater development which must take place in Canada if industry is to develop as we all desire to see it develop. We are living in an age of great combines and mergers and powerful monopolies that are able to compete more than successfully with their less fortunate smaller neighbours. Unless, therefore, government assistance is made available to the struggling smaller concerns they will simply have to succumb to the greater power of the competition they face.
In the United States this problem was met years ago by the establishment of the reconstruction finance corporation. The time is long overdue for Canada to have an extensive reconstruction finance corporation. When we stop to consider the experience we Albertans have had in trying to develop the oil industry in Alberta and now a gas industry, just to use those two as examples; when we remember that our men who began to develop the oil industry went to every concern in Canada and Great Britain in an endeavour to find capital with which to develop these oil resources and found that it was impossible to obtain capital from either one of these sources and finally had to go to the United States in order to get the necessary capital to drill the wells and develop these resources, these things alone should impress upon us the fact that it is utterly impossible for Canada to develop her industries and resources as she should unless she has the assistance of powerful government aid backed by no less a concern than the Bank of Canada itself.
What has already been said by the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Greenwood is sufficient; it is not necessary for me to repeat what they have said. I will simply say that the Social Credit group is heartily in favour of the act and wishes it to be extended with all possible speed and at just as great a scope of growth as is possible under the conditions that confront us.

Industrial Development Bank Act

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ENLARGE CLASSES OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should not like to let this occasion pass without saying a few words in connection with the industrial development bank, and I shall try to avoid any repetition of what I might otherwise have said. I happen to have seen the bank in action at close range, and there is no doubt about the very useful function it performs as part of our general financing set-up. I believe it fills very ably the gap between the legislation which enables our chartered banks to carry on certain phases of business and the system that exists in the United States which enables their local banking houses to take such security as mortgages on real property and to lend money on chattels and articles of that kind.
I think too the bank has filled a very useful function with respect to the financing of air companies. As a matter of fact, I might say that for a period of time it was most difficult for that type of company to obtain the necessary financing to cover the expansion of their services. There was a period in which the ordinary type of financing available through finance houses with respect to the acquisition of planes ceased to exist, and until this type of loan came along it was most difficult for such companies to add to their roster of planes.
I said once before and I should like to repeat that certainly if the bank is going to fulfil its true role it must be expanded. I might be sorry that some of this financing is not being carried out by the chartered institutions, but if this is the vehicle to provide this type of financing then very definitely, as has been suggested, it should be expanded from coast to coast. I am delighted to see that in a small way at least there is a beginning along that line. As a matter of fact, I am more delighted to know that the very loyal employees of the bank, who had a definite ceiling put on their future, now have the opportunity to have their services made much more use of in the expanding affairs of the bank.
If I may say one other thing, and I perhaps will refer to it when we come to one of the specific sections, I think there should be a considerable increase in the discretionary power of the local managers in this type of institution. I do not think it is something that should be carried on by a manager at Vancouver with a low discretionary limit of $5,000 or some type of limit of that kind, anything exceeding that amount having to be forwarded to the head office of the bank for approval. It seems to me that there should be greater manoeuvrability in the various offices of the bank in order to see that the servicing of the customers is done in

a quicker manner so that in the long run they will be much better satisfied with the services.
Generally speaking there is no doubt about the usefulness of the really essential function this bank is performing in our economy. I believe we welcome strongly the indication that this influence is to be spread on a much broader basis.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that I would be remiss in my duties if I did not say a few words on this item. As most hon. members of the house know, industrial development is badly needed in the maritime provinces, and it has been badly needed for some considerable time. I was in the house when this bank legislation was introduced, and I visualized that the bank was to be an instrument by means of which capital could be secured at lower rates of interest and on longer terms of repayment than could be obtained from the regular chartered banks. The name itself suggests that the intention of the legislation was to assist in industrial development and expansion.
However, it seems to me that the figures that are contained in this report and which were put on the record by the hon. member for Assiniboia confirm the old adage, "To him that hath shall be given", because in the central provinces where capital is available and where industrial expansion has gone on apace since the end of the war, it seems that is where the greatest amount of money has been lent by the industrial development bank for industrial expansion, I would assume in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
The reason I am interested at this time is to inform the house that in speaking recently to the Canadian Labour Congress in Toronto and commenting on resolutions that were before that convention setting out the difficulties and disabilities of the maritimes, the Prime Minister issued a challenge and said that the initiative for the solution of these problems rested with the maritimes themselves, and that when they laid the proper ground work and had recommendations to make, the federal government would be glad to help.
I should just like to say that a great deal of ground work has been done in the maritimes over the years. The Nova Scotia government have a department of industry. I notice they are running to the United States looking for money largely to help in developing some industry in that area.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ENLARGE CLASSES OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Saskatchewan does, too.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ENLARGE CLASSES OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
They must go somewhere. Apparently there is not any risk capital in

this country. When dealing with things all the way from a pulp mill to a pipe line you must go outside for the money or come with your hat in hand to the government and say, "You can establish the thing for us, but you do not have any say in the operation of it." However, we have tried in that end of the country. The government has set up a department of industry. In addition to that we have seen the formation of the Atlantic provinces economic council that is doing the economic surveys as to the possibility of the location of industry, as to marketing and what can be done. All that material is being assembled. In many communities there are industrial development boards. They are trying to raise some local money. But any project that is worth while is too big to be financed in the community.
I always understood that the industrial development bank was an instrument that should be available to the provincial governments, and that if they wanted to establish a project funds should be made available to the provincial government through this medium. The department of industry in Nova Scotia at least will make loans-they are not very substantial-to projects that are economically sound in the community; and when companies are formed and the legal formalities have been gone through, they can raise some money, but it is not adequate in most cases. I am wondering why under this legislation this bank could not be used as a public investment body for the purpose of assisting in areas where it is not so easy to raise capital.
During the years 1953, 1954 and 1955 the maritime provinces have been doing a great deal in regard to bringing about their own rehabilitation. But on looking at the report I notice that there is not even an office in the maritimes. The report lists the officers and supervisors. It sets out Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver; but for the Atlantic provinces it lists 901 Victoria Square, Montreal, Quebec. That is a long way from the maritimes.
In any case, this legislation is little known. Not much is done to advertise it. During the years it has been operating my conception has been that anyone who can qualify for a loan under the legislation setting up the industrial development bank can get that money at the chartered banks, because your collateral must be fairly substantial and fairly secure. Anyone whom I have seen apply and who did get his loan, could have got it from the chartered banks. I know quite a few people who were turned down and who told me that, as far as they were concerned, if they could have met the requirements of the industrial development bank they could have obtained
7, 1956
Industrial Development Bank Act the money at the regular chartered banks, but they just did not have that kind of credit.
There is another consideration. I do not think this bank is serving the purpose it should serve. The municipalities across this country are floating bond issues for school projects. They put their bonds on the market and in many instances they are sold in the United States, and they are losing 5 per cent to 8 per cent on the dollar.

speechtext: How could they do that?

speechtext: By them giving you 90 cents on your dollar for your bonds; that is how they do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

speechtext:
Not when you are floating bonds. If the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration were going to invest $100,000 in a community, I am sure he would not take bonds for $100,000 with no interest. He would naturally expect to make 4 per cent or 5 per cent or 6 per cent. Even the industrial development bank want 6 per cent on their dollar. Hence if you borrow $100,000 and you pay back that $100,000 plus interest, that is the same thing the small communities that are floating bonds are doing. Why could not the bond issues of municipalities be financed through an instrument like the industrial development bank?
I know that in the end of the country from which I come there were communities in which credit unions, out of the earnings of the workers, had to buy up bond issues to finance school projects. Of course over the long pull they will make money out of that, and that money is staying in the community. It is a thing I advocate; but the finances of credit unions are not adequate to handle such projects.
So far as I am concerned I go along with the hon. member for Assiniboia. It seems to me that most of our legislation in this country today is not national legislation. When you have offices across the country starting in Vancouver and ending in Montreal, you have not a national organization. The same thing could be said of most of the projects in which the federal government is engaged. It is true of the pipe line. Somebody says it is an across-Canada proposal, but it is not. It is coming from Alberta and ending in Montreal, yet everybody in this country will be expected to finance some of it out of taxation. That is true of the industrial development bank. If this bank is to serve the purposes I heard outlined when the legislation was introduced, then there should be offices in at least all the major cities across Canada.

speechtext: I have one or two questions I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant while we are on clause 1. Is it the opinion of the government that the word "goods" in paragraph (d), subparagraph (i) of the definition section would include ships and vessels?

I wonder
whether the parliamentary assistant would look at the wording of paragraph (d) (iii). It seems to me that there may be a surplus of language in this section starting at line 15. If we go back to the definition section we find that it says:

-in which is carried on the business of (iii) . . . the transportation of persons.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ENLARGE CLASSES OF LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: I have just one more question on that. I notice in the paragraph they refer to the amount of the investment and also to the character of the investment. What is the distinction between those two terms?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ENLARGE CLASSES OF LOANS, ETC.

The character is the type of security in which the bank is going to make its investment or take as security. Now, it could be real estate, the fixed asset of the business.
